items.title: Belonging: Sonia Gandhi’s memoir is from the heart, moving but playing it safe
items.summary: The picture in your head, as you read Sonia Gandhi's Belonging , can at first be black and white and grainy like the front cover, of her young face looking at an India of nearly 60 years ago, when she first came here for love. The picture gathers colour as you read on and find Sonia at home in India, slowly and almost hesitatingly growing into the Congress veteran she has become. Just like in politics, she seems to have inadvertently captured her extraordinary life, without really wanting to, in her from-the-heart memoir. The book, selling like it had been awaited forever, though it was announced only earlier this year, may have that kind of pull because it comes from one of India’s most important political figures. But it is her writing that sustains that pull and keeps the reader turning the pages. When nonfiction has this kind of effect it is lazily lauded as reading like fiction. But Sonia’s life, overwhelmed with untoward incidents, could easily have become a chaotic mess on paper.
